explanation: N225+ fires at phrase boundaries in running prose: activation is strongest on the token that closes a phrase - the token whose successor is a comma, full stop, semicolon, closing bracket or a linking preposition/conjunction ('of', 'to', 'in', 'and', 'but', 'than') - and grows with the length of the unit since the previous punctuation (13% of such tokens exceed half-max after 5+ tokens vs 5% right after punctuation), while falling to the floor when the same word sits mid-phrase (before a word continuation or a determiner+noun), just after punctuation, or after a matched word-order edit ('the weather was dry' 2.11 -> 'the dry weather was' 0.21). Its write only nudges high-frequency function words (' the' +1.3 nats, then ' it', ' your', ' these') and suppresses rare word-continuation fragments, leaving the top-1 token unchanged at 89% of peaks (protocol lookahead KL 9e-4, so retrospective); mid-word fragments of byte-mangled non-Latin text also peak and remain an unexplained leftover.
